title: Design the acre language
body: What an `.acre` file looks like: how it declares the canvas and the objects on it, and later how each object changes over time. Jack settles the syntax by writing files in a working version and reacting to them. Each version goes into `crates/acre/src/lang` and `scene` once it is small enough to try. Over those versions, pin down the top-level shape of a file, how time is written (seconds, frames, or both), and how a property is animated between two values.

notes.author: Jack Roddy/89ec73b0
notes.text: Settled so far, syntax still open: canvas coordinates are pixels with the origin top-left. Time is seconds in the model; the frame index belongs to the renderer. The domain is arrays, matrices, grids and simple plots, so text in cells and on axes is in the first version. First examples to design the syntax against: an array of numbers being sorted (highlight the compared pair, swap them) and a line plot that draws itself with points appearing.

notes.author: Jack Roddy/89ed765a
notes.text:
Jack wants joined editing in the acre GUI. The GUI holds a text editor beside the render. Editing the text re-renders the scene. Dragging or stretching an object in the render rewrites the source text. To support that, `lang` and `scene` need four things:

- a parser that keeps comments and whitespace, so acre can rewrite one literal and leave the rest of the file as typed
- the source span of every value in the scene
- an id on every scene object that carries through to the primitives it draws
- a way for `scene` to say which object is under a point on the canvas

A value computed from other values has no single literal to rewrite. A grid cell whose x comes from its index is one. The syntax design has to say what a drag does to such a value. Two options so far are to refuse the drag, or to rewrite the nearest literal that feeds it, such as the grid's origin. Neither is chosen.

Static images, diagrams and plots are the main use. Simple animations still matter.

notes.author: Jack Roddy/89ed765a
notes.text:
Jack can't judge a syntax on paper. He wants a language he can run and react to, with still images settled before animation. The syntax uses braces and should look nothing like Python.

v0 is the first version to play with. A file is a tree of nodes. A node is a kind, an optional name and a braced body of properties (`key values;`) and child nodes. The parser gives nothing a meaning. `scene` interprets each node kind, so a change of vocabulary leaves the parser alone. The node kinds in v0 are `canvas`, `box`, `ellipse`, `line`, `arrow` and `text`. v0 has no time.

Three earlier candidates are set aside until still images work. They were objects plus a timeline, inline keyframes on every property, and sequenced steps.

notes.author: Jack Roddy/89ed765a
notes.text: v0 landed in f5a9de6. `crates/acre/examples/layers.acre` is its first example file.

notes.author: Jack Roddy/cd2d1020
notes.text:
v1 adds the nodes the `PrefixEncoder` figure (acre-de907c) needed. Nothing in it is committed yet.

| node or property | what it does | why |
|---|---|---|
| `row` | cells on a grid of equal units, each covering a whole number of units | a 64-bit word is 21 cells of 3 bits and one of 1, so a cell's width has to follow its bits |
| `cells "G" "A" ...;` and `cell { ... }` children | the list covers the common case, and a child cell overrides span, fill, stroke or note | 21 cells written as nodes would be 21 lines per row |
| `palette NAME { symbol "A" #color "001"; }` | fills and notes by cell text | each character keeps one colour and its code across every row |
| `brace` with `over ROW A B` | a curly or square bracket along cells A to B | the figure labels runs of cells, and computing their pixels by hand would break when a row moves |
| `ruler` | a numbered scale of units | bit numbers from 63 down to 0 under a key |
| `from ROW N side` on `line` and `arrow` | ends a line at a cell, or at the middle of one of its sides | the roll panel joins cell k of one row to cell k-1 of the next |
| `font` on the canvas and on any text | `mono`, `sans`, `sans-bold`, `sans-italic` | prose in Noto Sans, code names in monospace |
| `dash`, `radius`, `\n` in strings | dashed strokes, rounded boxes, multi-line text | |

The example `crates/acre/examples/prefix-encoder.acre` came from a script that computed the keys and coordinates. Writing the file by hand would mean placing about 300 objects with numbers worked out on paper. The language has no arithmetic, loops or relative placement, and those three are what a hand-written figure of this size would need.

notes.author: Jack Roddy/cd2d1020
notes.text:
v2 makes a figure the size of the `PrefixEncoder` one writable by hand. `crates/acre/examples/prefix-encoder.acre` is now hand-written in 171 lines. The generated version was 229 lines of absolute coordinates.

- `let NAME VALUES;` on the canvas. A bare word equal to a let name stands for its values in any property. The substitution runs before `scene` reads a node, in `scene/expand.rs`. It has no scoping, so a let name shadows any word value of the same spelling, such as `right` or `show`.
- `style NAME { ... }` and `style A B;` on a node. A node's own property wins over a style's, and a later style over an earlier one. Styles reach nested nodes such as a row's `cell` children.
- `group { at X Y; ... }` moves the numbers in every `at`, `from` and `to` inside it. Names stay global, and an end that names a thing uses where that thing already is.
- `at NAME DX DY` starts from a shape's or a row's top-left corner, and `at ROW N DX DY` from a cell's. A row name followed by exactly one number reads as a cell, so `at row -60 14` has to give both numbers.
- `chars "GATC"` adds a cell per character.
- `repeat N` on `line` and `arrow` draws N copies, adding one to every cell index on each copy. The 20 lines of the roll panel are one node.
- A palette `symbol` takes a text color after its note, for white text on dark cells.

The derived-values box still takes 15 `text` nodes for a three-column table. A `table` node, or text that mixes colours within a line, would shorten it. Neither is built.
